title: The Wizard, The Pie, and The Sprite
markdown:
In Whisperwind Peaks the paths snaked through ancient firs, and villages nested in the shadows of tall mountains. Cedric the wizard lived at the foot of the highest peak in a cottage that smelled of dried herbs and the rustle of spell scrolls. Vials crowded the windowsills. Books made tottering towers. It was a cozy mess, and he liked it that way.

Every day Moss, his black jackdaw, hunted shiny buttons, beetle wings, and smooth pebbles to hoard among the books. Moss’s eyes gleamed with mischief. Cedric loved the dance of runes and whispered words. He also kept a small, secret wish: to cast a spell so obvious, so brilliant, that even the serious mountain goats would nod. His magic, he feared, was too quiet. Too easy to miss.

The village elders knew he loved quiet study. That was why they asked him to mind the stall at Sunstone Market while Old Man Hemlock took a nap. Cedric agreed with a sweep of his robe. He pictured the usual bundles of herbs becoming a wonder of sparkling delights. People would marvel. The goats, if they happened by, might even nod.

The market buzzed. Coins clattered. Elara the baker’s honey cakes made the air taste of warmth. Cedric took out a small polished agate, a gift from a gnome, and whispered a charm for super brightness.

“Let this stone shine like a thousand suns.”

The agate stayed dull. Nearby, a plain grey pebble the size of a sparrow’s egg flared emerald, pulsing among the vegetables and wool as if it had been waiting for an invitation to be silly. Cedric’s face went hot. He hid the pebble under rosemary.

“Well,” he muttered. “Unexpected.”

Moss, on his shoulder, gave a knowing caw and nudged his ear.

Then Elara rushed from her stall, apron white with flour. “My moonberry pie! Vanished from the cooling rack!” The bake-off was tomorrow. Whispers ran the crowd: pixies from the Whispering Woods, a griffin, a bold badger with a sweet tooth. Elara wrung her hands. Facing the judges without her masterpiece felt like arriving at a party without a name.

Cedric, still embarrassed and hungry to prove himself, puffed out his chest. “Don’t worry, Elara. I’ll use a locating charm. My magic is particular, but it can find a pie.”

He pointed his wand at the glowing pebble.

“Seek and find, by light divine, bring back the pie, this treasure of thine! Let not a crumb escape my sight!”

The pebble pulsed. A faint green trail unspooled through the stalls like a tiny comet’s tail. Cedric followed, beaming. Moss fluttered above, scanning. Past socks. Past apples. Then the trail ended at a single muddy sock tucked beneath a farmer’s cart.

Cedric stared. Moss tilted his head. It was not a pie. Not even a crumb of one.

A clear, musical voice cut through the murmuring. “A locating charm, you say? And it found a sock? Interesting. Perhaps it wants to knit itself a new pair.”

Fen, the witch from the cliffs, had a kind face and eyes that sparkled with amusement. Her magic was practical. Her wit was dry. A friendly rivalry often sparked between them, each certain their way was best for the valley’s muddles.

“Perhaps,” Fen went on, friendly and a little challenging, “scent and careful watching would have worked better. I suspect a creature of habit, not a clever trickster. My wards detected no unusual magic. Only sugar, and a faint desperation, toward the Old Oak grove.”

Cedric felt the blush climb his neck. The pebble hummed in his palm, as if agreeing with someone else.

“My spells sometimes have minds of their own,” he admitted. “This pebble enchants the most useful things in the most unexpected ways.”

Fen chuckled, a sound like dry leaves. “Exactly. My tracking uses scent and the natural world. It has led me this way.” She pointed to a cluster of ancient oaks at the market’s edge.

Moss, who had been circling, swooped and nudged a loose patch of moss near the largest oak’s roots. Cedric knelt. Warm moonberries filled the air. He pushed the moss aside. A small hollow. Soft rustling. The moss under his hand felt strangely yielding.

Inside, curled asleep, was a forest sprite no bigger than Cedric’s hand, leafy hair tangled around his face. Beside him, a little messy but whole, sat Elara’s moonberry pie. The sprite stirred. Large innocent eyes. A wooden spoon. Purple filling on his cheek.

Pip explained, in apologetic chirps and whistles, that he had been very hungry. He had wandered too far from the woods. The pie had smelled so wonderfully sweet he had not managed to resist. He had not meant to cause trouble.

Cedric looked at those pleading eyes and the half-eaten pie, and the wish for grand magic went quiet. He remembered his own eagerness to impress. Fen’s rivalry with him seemed, suddenly, a small thing.

“Well, Pip,” Fen said softly. “A lesson in asking nicely. And offering to help Elara with her chores in return for a slice. I am sure she would share, if you promised not to sneak off with the whole thing.”

Cedric lifted the pie as if it were a sleeping bird. “And perhaps,” he said, “instead of a spell to find lost things, I should practice a charm for sharing. And for understanding.”

He tapped the glowing pebble politely and asked it to dim. It pulsed once, a soft contented shimmer, and obeyed. Moss ruffled his feathers, hopped onto Cedric’s hand, and nudged a finger as if to say the sprite had been far more interesting than any button.

The market found its hum again, relief mixed with wonder. Elara, though a little annoyed about her pie, could not stay angry at someone the size of a teacup. Fen gave Cedric a nod that acknowledged the new thought without making a speech of it.

“A creature’s heart,” she said, “is often simpler than any complex spell.”

Cedric smiled, truly. “Who could have guessed that a bit of moonlight and a bit of hunger would lead us to a sprite, a sock, and a shared pie?”

They cut what remained. Elara wrapped a slice for Pip and a smaller one for Moss, who inspected it as if it might be a pebble in disguise. Hemlock’s stall sold its herbs without a single sparkle. The mountain goats, when they passed, did not nod. Cedric found he did not mind.

Ever since then he has still loved his research, the patterns of old knowledge stacked in tottering towers. He has also learned the quiet charm of a kind word, the joy of a shared slice, and the steady wisdom of a jackdaw who always seems to know when a bit of gentle looking is the magic that everyday life actually needs. The emerald pebble lives under the rosemary jar at home, dull until asked, and Cedric does not ask it to shine like a thousand suns.
characters: Cedric (a wizard), Moss (a jackdaw), Fen (a witch)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
